title: CMS Finalizes Rule to Help More Organs Reach Patients and Strengthen Accountability for Organ Procurement Organizations
content: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 30, 2026 Contact: HHS Press Office 202-690-6343 Submit a Request for Comment CMS Finalizes Rule to Help More Organs Reach Patients and Strengthen Accountability for Organ Procurement Organizations WASHINGTON, D.C.—OCTOBER 30, 2026—The U.S. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS), through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), has finalized a rule to help more donated organs reach patients by strengthening oversight of Organ Procurement Organizations (OPOs). OPOs connect donor hospitals and transplant programs by securing authorization for donations, recovering organs, and coordinating safe, timely delivery for transplantation. This rule builds upon President Trump’s 2019 Executive Order, Advancing American Kidney Health, and helps advance a key goal of the Department’s Kidney Care National Plan to reform organ transplantationWhile more than 49,000 transplants were performed in the United States in 2025, over 100,000 Americans are waiting for lifesaving transplants. To improve access to transplants, the final rule allows high-performing OPOs to compete for multiple donation service areas, clarifies OPO recertification procedures, and reinforces longstanding process performance standards.“Every donated organ carries the chance to save a life,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are holding failing organizations accountable, strengthening patient safeguards, and helping high-performing organizations reach more patients. We will honor donors’ gifts by demanding results.”“Americans waiting for lifesaving transplants cannot afford poor performance by OPOs, and CMS is committed to holding these organizations accountable,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “With today’s new rule, CMS is building on the success of organ procurement reforms from the first Trump Administration to promote clearer documentation, higher donation rates, and swifter consequences for bad actors.”The final rule establishes clear requirements when one OPO takes over from another and strengthens oversight of unsafe practices. It also changes how CMS measures transplant performance so that pancreata used only for islet cell research do not count as transplants. This will make sure that OPO transplant performance scores reflect organs transplanted into patients.Key provisions of the final OPO rule include:Enhanced oversight of unsound medical practices: The rule defines “unsound medical practices” to clarify when CMS may use its existing authority to immediately decertify a noncompliant OPO to protect patients.Adverse events and quality improvement: OPOs now have clearer guidance to spot, investigate, and prevent adverse events.Pancreata for islet cell research: A donor whose pancreas is procured only for islet cell research continues to count toward the OPO’s donation rate, but pancreata used for islet cell research no longer count toward the transplantation rate in the absence of a transplant.Documentation of research organs: OPOs must now track and record what happens to organs sent for research, including pancreata used for islet cell research.Licensure: An OPO’s medical director must hold a license in at least one state or territory the OPO serves.Decertification pathways: CMS clearly spells out the circumstances under which CMS may decertify an OPO.Appeals process: The rule codifies a process for discretionary CMS Administrator review of hearing officer decisions and updates appeals timeframes.Competition and donation service area transitions: Outgoing OPOs must cooperate with incoming ones, and incoming OPOs must submit a transition plan with progress updates to facilitate uninterrupted organ donation operations in the service area.Certification requirements: The rule removes a requirement limiting certification to OPOs recertified between 2002 and 2005.Today’s action builds on the first Trump Administration’s 2020 OPO rule, which established transparent, reliable, and objective performance measures and increased competition for open donation service areas. Since CMS issued that rule, organ donations have increased by 36% nationwide, transplants have increased by 30%, and the number of lowest-performing OPOs continues to decline.The OPO final rule complements HHS' recently released Kidney Care National Plan, a comprehensive strategy to prevent kidney failure before it begins, restore competition and choice in dialysis care, and reform the nation's organ transplant system. Further information on the Kidney Care National Plan is available at: https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/kidney-care-national-plan-fact-sheet.html.The final rule is available in the Federal Register at: https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-22381.pdfView the final rule fact sheet at: https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicare-medicaid-programs-organ-procurement-organizations-conditions-coverage-revisions-conditions ### Note: All HHS press releases, fact sheets and other news materials are available in our Press Room.Like HHS on Facebook, follow HHS on X @HHSgov, @SecKennedy, and sign up for HHS Email Updates.Last revised: October 30, 2026

title: HHS Final Rule Amends Section 504 Regulations to Codify Statutory Exclusions from the Definition of Disability
content: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 30, 2026 Contact: HHS Press Office 202-690-6343 Submit a Request for Comment HHS Final Rule Amends Section 504 Regulations to Codify Statutory Exclusions from the Definition of Disability Rule Clarifies That Gender Dysphoria Not Resulting from Physical Impairments Is Excluded Under the Rehabilitation ActWASHINGTON, D.C.—OCTOBER 30, 2026—The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) today published a final rule clarifying that, under HHS regulations, gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments does not qualify as a disability under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Section 504). This rule applies to all programs and activities that receive HHS funding, aligning the agency's regulations with the exclusions Congress wrote into law.HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. announced the proposed rule at an event in Washington, DC in December 2025.“My uncle Ted Kennedy was the primary author of the Americans with Disabilities Act and the 1978 amendments that strengthened the Rehabilitation Act. The Biden-era pronouncements that indicated gender dysphoria may be a disability served the commercial interests of a predatory, multi-billion-dollar industry and betrayed the original intention of those laws,” said Secretary Kennedy. “Congress defined which conditions qualify for protection as disabilities under federal law, and HHS has a duty to faithfully apply the law as written. This final rule restores clarity to our regulations, respects the distinctions Congress established, and ensures that HHS administers Section 504 according to its statutory text. The Trump Administration will continue to bring transparency, accountability, and fidelity to the law back to federal policymaking.”This update resolves an ambiguity in the 2024 Final Rule and ensures the rule aligns with the best reading of the law. The preamble to the 2024 Final Rule suggested that gender dysphoria could qualify as a disability, although the regulation was silent on the issue. In April 2025, HHS issued a notice in the Federal Register underscoring that the preamble has no force or effect of law and the regulation did not address gender dysphoria. Today’s rule aligns HHS’s implementing regulations with the statutory exclusion by determining that gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments include gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments.OCR enforces Section 504, which prohibits programs and activities that receive federal financial assistance from discriminating against individuals based on their disability. Several conditions were excluded from coverage when the law was written, including gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments. The 2026 Final Rule adds those statutory exclusions to HHS’ Section 504 regulation at 45 C.F.R. § 84.4(g) and makes clear that gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments falls within the exclusions.“For decades, HHS’ Section 504 regulations have defined disability consistently with the words Congress chose. This rule ensures recipients of HHS funding follow those definitions, eliminating confusion for the people they serve and restoring confidence in the statute,” said HHS OCR Director Paula M. Stannard.HHS published the proposed rule on December 19, 2025. During the comment period, it received more than 380 comments from private citizens, healthcare providers, educators, disability advocacy organizations, faith-based organizations, professional associations, states, and members of Congress. OCR reviewed every comment and responded to the significant issues raised in the preamble to the final rule.Although the clarification only affects one provision of the rule, it serves multiple goals:Updates HHS Section 504 regulation to identify the conditions Congress excluded from the definitions of “disability” and “individual with a disability.”Clarifies that gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments is excluded from coverage.Clarifies the existing obligations of organizations and entities that receive HHS funding.The rule is consistent with Executive Order 14168 and the administration’s deregulatory agenda outlined in Executive Order 14219.Read the final rule in the Federal Register.If you believe that you or someone else has been discriminated against in programs or activities that HHS directly operates or for which HHS provides federal financial assistance, you may file a complaint with OCR.OCR enforces protections based on race, color, national origin, disability, age, sex, religion, and the exercise of conscience.Follow HHS OCR on X at @HHSOCR. ### Note: All HHS press releases, fact sheets and other news materials are available in our Press Room.Like HHS on Facebook, follow HHS on X @HHSgov, @SecKennedy, and sign up for HHS Email Updates.Last revised: October 30, 2026

title: FDA Issues Final Guidance on Prescription Drug Apps and Software
content: FDA News Release FDA Issues Final Guidance on Prescription Drug Apps and Software New policy clarifies when app content requires FDA review and how drug-connected software must be described on medication labels More Press Announcements For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today released final guidance establishing a clear framework for how drug companies can develop, distribute, and label apps used alongside their prescription medicines. The guidance ends longstanding uncertainty by providing recommendations about when app content is subject to FDA submission requirements, when an app should be mentioned on a drug’s official label, and what companies should submit to the agency.“Mobile apps are playing a growing role in how patients manage their medications and health conditions,” said Captain Chris Wheeler, Pharm.D., Director of the Division of Medical Policy Programs within FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “This guidance helps ensure that the information these tools provide is accurate, evidence-based, and clearly communicated to both patients and their providers.”The guidance addresses three key questions for industry: when app content is treated as FDA-required labeling versus promotional labeling, when an app should be referenced in a drug’s official prescribing information, and what companies should submit to FDA when they distribute app content to users.The guidance identifies two categories of companion software:Apps connected to a medical device (such as an app paired with an asthma inhaler) generally should be described on the drug’s official prescribing label, given the central role the software plays in how the medicine is used.Standalone apps (such as symptom trackers, dose reminders, or health coaching tools) should appear on the prescribing label if the company can show the app is essential for safe and effective use or can demonstrate a meaningful clinical benefit. In most cases, content a companion app displays to users will be treated as promotional material, consistent with how the FDA handles other drug advertising.“This guidance reflects FDA’s commitment to responsible, risk-proportionate oversight of digital health, an area that is a key priority for the agency and is evolving rapidly and holds significant promise for improving patient care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “By aligning our approach across drug and device centers, we are giving developers a clear and consistent pathway to bring safe, effective digital health technologies to patients.”“Companion apps are quickly moving beyond simple dose reminders toward tools that adapt to each patient,” said Jared Seehafer, M.S., FDA Deputy Commissioner for Technology. “Finalizing this guidance gives drug companies and their technology partners a stable foundation to build on as these technologies advance and helps ensure patients and providers can trust the information they receive.”This guidance also reflects the FDA’s ongoing commitment to modernizing its regulatory framework to keep pace with rapidly evolving digital health technologies. By providing clear, practical recommendations for both drug-connected software and standalone software, the agency aims to reduce unnecessary uncertainty for developers and manufacturers while preserving the safety and effectiveness standards that patients and healthcare providers rely on.The final guidance is available here. title: FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
content: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Groundbreaking therapy provides additional treatment option that fights the disease at its source, not only its symptoms More Press Announcements For Immediate Release: October 30, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), a rare disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that leads to the formation of small, wart-like growths in the patient’s airways. This approval, the first for a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy in the U.S., offers patients a new therapeutic option that targets the root cause of RRP and has been shown to reduce the burden of surgical intervention, representing an important step forward for a patient population with limited treatment options.“Adults living with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often face an exhausting and relentless cycle of repeated surgeries, managing their disease, but never truly escaping it. Today’s approval represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough: a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body’s own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP,” said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER). “For patients, that could mean fewer surgeries, fewer disruptions, and more time living their lives on their own terms. The FDA is proud to help bring that possibility within reach.”The agency based this accelerated approval on clinical trial data showing Voceryq helps reduce the frequency of surgical procedures required to remove growths in adult patients with RRP — an intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The accelerated approval pathway allows the FDA to approve drugs or biologics for serious or life-threatening conditions based on an effect on a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit.RRP is a rare, chronic disease in which wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11 form in the airways, most often around the larynx (voice box), particularly the vocal cords. These growths, called papillomas, can cause symptoms like hoarseness, chronic cough, and voice changes, and in severe cases can spread to other parts of the respiratory tract, causing difficulty breathing. While surgery can remove the growths, there is no cure, and the virus persists in the tissue even after the growths are removed, so patients often need repeated procedures over many years. In some cases, RRP carries a risk of becoming cancerous over time. Voceryq is a recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that delivers two plasmids (small pieces of DNA originally derived from bacteria) into the body’s cells, one of which contains the genetic instructions for specific HPV proteins and the other an immune response-enhancing molecule called IL-12. The therapy is designed to stimulate the immune system to respond to and attack cells infected by the specific types of HPV that cause RRP (types 6 and 11). Voceryq is administered via intramuscular (IM) injection using the CELLECTRA 5PSP Device, which delivers the dose and facilitates electroporation, a technique which uses brief electrical pulses to temporarily and reversibly create pores in the cell membranes to enable the delivery of Voceryq into the body’s cells.The safety and effectiveness of Voceryq was evaluated in an open-label multicenter clinical trial in 32 adults diagnosed with RRP. Eligible patients had two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the 12 months prior to Voceryq treatment, including a scheduled surgery at trial entry. Seven (27%) out of 26 patients who had at least three baseline surgeries did not require any surgery intervention during the first year after treatment.The most commonly reported adverse reactions to Voceryq were injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension (high blood pressure), nausea, and dizziness. Adverse effects associated with the electroporation technique may include brief muscle contractions or tetany, temporary bleeding at the administration site, anxiety, vasovagal reactions including lightheadedness and dizziness, transient changes in creatine phosphokinase, erythema (skin redness) at the injection site, and pain at the injection site.The FDA granted Voceryq Breakthrough and Orphan Drug designations. The FDA granted accelerated approval of Voceryq to Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc. title: FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery
content: FDA News Release FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery More Press Announcements For Immediate Release: October 19, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for a new use of the immunotherapy Jemperli (dostarlimab-gxly) that may allow some patients with locally advanced rectal cancer to avoid common treatments that can have a lasting impact on their daily life.Patients with locally advanced rectal cancer often receive chemotherapy and radiation prior to surgery, which can affect bowel, urinary, and sexual function, as well as fertility. Surgery also carries risks of serious, sometimes life-threatening complications, including poor healing and leaks where the bowel is reconnected, and in some patients, permanent colostomy.“The FDA is committed to closing the gap between scientific progress and patient access, and that commitment has to show up not just in policy, but in the pace of our work,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “American patients deserve timely access to innovative treatments, and the Trump Administration is making that a reality. Completing this review nearly 4 months ahead of schedule means some patients who might otherwise be preparing for surgery, radiation or chemotherapy may now have a different conversation with their doctor.”Today’s approval is for Jemperli used alone in adults with previously untreated stage II or stage III locally advanced rectal cancer. At these stages, the cancer has grown into nearby tissue or reached nearby lymph nodes but has not spread to distant organs. To be eligible, patients’ tumors must be mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), as determined by an FDA-authorized test. Published estimates suggest that approximately 3% of locally advanced rectal cancers are dMMR or MSI-H.Both terms describe a defect in the way cancer cells correct errors when copying their DNA. Normally, a built-in repair system catches and fixes these mistakes. When the system does not work properly, errors accumulate and create proteins the immune system can recognize, making these tumors particularly vulnerable to immunotherapy.Jemperli works by blocking a signal that cancer cells use to shield themselves from the immune system. Specifically, it targets a protein called PD-1 on immune cells.“Standard treatment for rectal cancer has major life-changing effects. For certain types of rectal cancer, this approval represents a groundbreaking option that avoids surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. This represents a significant benefit for patients and their families,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence. “The FDA is acting on emerging evidence to bring new approaches to patients sooner, while requiring further studies to confirm that these treatments provide lasting benefits.”The FDA based its decision on interim results from AZUR-1 (NCT05723562), a phase 2 study evaluating Jemperli alone in 154 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. In the study, patients received up to nine doses of Jemperli, given every 3 weeks over 6 months. After a median follow-up of more than 2 years — meaning at least half of patients had been monitored for that long — almost three-fourths of patients had not needed surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Longer follow-up is needed to understand the duration of response and how often the cancer returns.An earlier study at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (NCT04165772) evaluated Jemperli alone in 50 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. None of the patients had detectable signs of cancer after Jemperli treatment, and nearly all patients (93%) maintained that cancer-free status for at least 12 months. Of the 27 patients followed for at least 3 years, only one had their cancer return, and it recurred in the same area.Jemperli can cause the immune system to attack healthy organs and tissues. These reactions can be severe or fatal. The most common side effects, reported in at least 15% of patients treated for this type of rectal cancer, were fatigue, rash, diarrhea and itching.The FDA granted Priority Review to the application and Breakthrough Therapy designation to Jemperli for the treatment of dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. This action marks the 11th approval of a drug reviewed under the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher pilot program, which aims to help accelerate the review of therapies that address national public health priorities. Because this is an accelerated approval based on interim trial results, the sponsor must continue following patients to show these responses create lasting clinical benefit.The approval was granted to GSK. title: FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment
content: FDA News Release FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment New treatment may allow some patients to maintain viral control after stopping all hepatitis B therapy More Press Announcements For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis. Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B. Hibsago is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have been taking HBV antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed levels of HBV in their blood and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less, as determined by an FDA-authorized test. “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” said Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.”Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago works by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins, helping reduce the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body.The FDA also authorized the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to aid in the selection of patients with chronic HBV infection for treatment with antiviral therapy in accordance with the FDA approved drug labeling and to assist in monitoring patients throughout the course of treatment. Researchers studied Hibsago in two clinical trials that compared it with a placebo, an inactive treatment. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. Patients take it alongside their existing hepatitis B medicine and continue that medicine for at least 24 weeks after their last Hibsago injection. Some patients may then be able to stop their existing medicine if they meet certain health and lab test requirements.Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood. Hibsago has a boxed warning for serious liver reactions as well as low platelet counts, which can increase the risk of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Hibsago also has warnings for worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, and serious risks if the injection is not administered properly. Patients need regular blood tests and follow up with their healthcare provider before and during treatment to monitor these risks. The most common side effects, excluding laboratory abnormalities, are injection site reactions, fever, fatigue and headache. The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review. The approval was granted to GSK plc. title: FDA Approves Once-Weekly Generic Hormone Therapy Patch for Women
content: FDA News Release FDA Approves Once-Weekly Generic Hormone Therapy Patch for Women More Press Announcements For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration yesterday approved the first generic of Climara Pro (estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system, 0.045 mg per day/0.015 mg), a transdermal hormone therapy patch for women with an intact uterus applied once a week. The approval aligns with FDA’s Public Health Pillar: Increasing Access to Affordable Medicines & Medical Products.“Menopause is a universal experience for women, and it can greatly affect a person’s quality of life. This approval makes effective treatment more accessible,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Approvals like this reflect FDA’s ongoing commitment to expanding American patient access to safe, affordable, high-quality medications.”The generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system is therapeutically equivalent to Climara Pro, which is indicated for use in women with an intact uterus for:Treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopausePrevention of postmenopausal osteoporosisClimara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system contain both estrogen and progestogen in a single patch; this differs from estrogen-only patches commonly used in menopause treatment. Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are specifically approved for women with an intact uterus, as the progestogen component is included to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia that can occur with estrogen use alone.“Once-weekly dosing can make a real difference in how patients manage their care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “A patch offers a convenient alternative to daily oral medications, which may help patients stay on track with their treatment.”Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are contraindicated in patients with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; breast cancer or a history of breast cancer; estrogen-dependent neoplasia; active deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE) or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease or a history of these conditions; known anaphylactic reaction or angioedema or hypersensitivity to estradiol and levonorgestrel; hepatic impairment or disease; and protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or other thrombophilic disorders.The most common adverse reactions (greater than or equal to 5%) are: application site reaction, vaginal bleeding, breast pain, upper respiratory infection, back pain, depression, pain, headache and flu syndrome.In the U.S., nine out of 10 prescriptions filled are for generic drugs. Increasing the availability of generic drugs helps to create competition in the marketplace, which then helps to make treatment more affordable and increases access to healthcare for more patients. Learn more about the FDA Drug Competition Action Plan.Climara Pro is a registered trademark of Bayer. The FDA approved Zydus Pharmaceuticals (USA) Inc.’s Estradiol and Levonorgestrel Transdermal System. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products. ### Content current as of: 10/20/2026 Regulated Product(s) Drugs Follow FDA Follow @US_FDA on X Follow FDA on Facebook Follow @FDAMedia on X

title: FDA Launches the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to Develop a Holistic, Fit-For-Purpose Framework for Rare Disease Drug Development
content: FDA News Release FDA Launches the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to Develop a Holistic, Fit-For-Purpose Framework for Rare Disease Drug Development Effort begins by Soliciting Public Feedback More Press Announcements For Immediate Release: October 14, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a division within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), today announced the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to reimagine the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. As outlined in a new white paper, the Initiative will develop an optimized, fit-for-purpose framework that reflects the realities of rare disease drug development by considering the nuances of each disease, patient needs, product type and the evidence that can be realistically generated in small patient populations.To solicit feedback on the Rare Disease Framework Initiative from patients and disease advocates, industry, and others, the FDA will host an October 28 meeting at the FDA’s White Oak campus. The meeting will be facilitated by the Reagan-Udall Foundation for the FDA.“Americans with rare diseases cannot afford a regulatory system that treats every condition the same,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump, FDA is rethinking rare disease drug development by putting patients at the center and matching regulatory requirements to the realities of small patient populations. We will remove unnecessary barriers, embrace cutting-edge science, and accelerate promising treatments while upholding FDA’s rigorous standards.” “Patients and families living with rare diseases have few or no approved treatment options, and the burden of uncertainty can extend across every part of their lives,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “As we learn more about rare diseases and better understand the breadth of suffering they cause, we must ensure that America’s regulatory system remains at the forefront — prepared to respond to emerging science, anticipate the needs of patients and families, and help bring safe and effective therapies to those who need them. The FDA will fight hard for patients by building a more consistent, predictable, and innovative approach to rare disease drug development while maintaining the rigorous standards Americans expect from the FDA.”The FDA has long used regulatory flexibility and developed targeted programs to support innovation in the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. These efforts have led to meaningful advances for patients and families. Nevertheless, with only 5% or so of rare conditions having an FDA-approved treatment, the FDA agrees with patients, drug developers, and providers that more must be done to speed the development of safe and effective treatments for rare diseases. In developing the framework, the FDA is committed to the following:Providing greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in regulatory decision-making through tailored guidance and transparent communication.Embedding the patient’s voice both early, and at clearly defined milestones, in the drug development and review process.Further leveraging external expertise to support customization of regulatory review.Building shared resources, robust training, and institutional knowledge on rare disease drug development and review.Applying risk-based approaches, particularly to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review and pre-approval inspections.Championing the use of cutting-edge science, novel methods and innovative statistical approaches in rare disease drug development.The Initiative is led by the FDA’s Rare Disease Innovation Hub, partnering with the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.“Patients with rare diseases and their families deserve a regulatory process that addresses the uniqueness of each of their conditions while maintaining the FDA’s rigorous standards,” said the Hub’s Director, Amy Comstock Rick, J.D. “A bold vision to reimagine the framework for rare disease drug development that builds on key learnings and milestones is necessary to meet this moment. This new framework will enhance consistency and predictability for both sponsors and for patients.”Further opportunities to provide input will follow the public meeting, including sector-specific roundtables, Requests for Information, and internal FDA feedback sessions. This feedback will inform the detailed development of a new framework, which might include potential new or revised guidance, revisions to regulations, staff training, and organizational changes.Additional Resources• FDA Rare Disease Innovation Hub• Rare Disease Framework Media:FDA Request for Comment202-690-6343 Consumer:888-INFO-FDA The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. title: New oral GLP-1 medicine for weight management and type 2 diabetes
content: New oral GLP-1 medicine for weight management and type 2 diabetes 16 October 2026 Once-daily tablet provides an alternative to other oral and injectable GLP-1 medicines NewsHumanMedicines Page contentsPage contents Related content Contact point Related medicine information EMA has recommended granting a marketing authorisation in the European Union for Foundayo (orforglipron), an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist for weight management and treatment of type 2 diabetes in adults. For weight management, Foundayo is used alongside a healthy diet and physical activity in adults with obesity (see note 2) or overweight (see note 3) who have at least one weight-related health problem. For type 2 diabetes, Foundayo is used alongside a healthy diet and physical activity in adults with type 2 diabetes whose blood glucose levels are not sufficiently controlled. It can be used alone when metformin is not appropriate, or together with other diabetes medicines. Obesity and overweight affect more than 2.5 billion people worldwide (see note 4) and increase the risk of serious health problems, including cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. In 2021, excess body weight was associated with around 4 million deaths and 129 million disability-adjusted life years worldwide (see note 5). Diabetes affects approximately 589 million adults (20 to 79 years) globally, with type 2 diabetes accounting for approximately 90% of all cases worldwide (see note 6). People with type 2 diabetes are at increased risk of complications such as heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, nerve damage and vision loss. Foundayo can only be obtained with a prescription and will be available as a tablet taken once daily, providing an alternative to injectable and other oral GLP-1 receptor agonists. It can be taken at any time of day, with or without food. Treatment starts at a low dose, which is gradually increased according to the patient’s response and how well they tolerate the medicine. The active substance in Foundayo, orforglipron, is a small, non-peptide molecule that activates the receptor for glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). GLP-1 is a natural hormone involved in controlling appetite and blood glucose levels. As a non-peptide medicine, orforglipron is developed to be taken orally. By activating these receptors, orforglipron reduces appetite and increases feelings of fullness, helping people eat less and lose weight. It also lowers blood glucose by helping the pancreas release more insulin when blood glucose levels are high, reducing levels of glucagon (a hormone that raises blood glucose) and helping the body respond better to insulin. EMA’s recommendation for Foundayo in weight management is based on two studies involving 4,740 adults with obesity or overweight. One study included adults without type 2 diabetes but another weight-related health problem, while the other included adults with type 2 diabetes. After 72 weeks, participants treated with Foundayo lost around 5% to 11% of their body weight, depending on the dose of Foundayo they took, compared with around 2% to 2.5% in those who took placebo. For type 2 diabetes, Foundayo was evaluated in four main studies involving 3,765 adults whose blood glucose was not adequately controlled with diet and physical activity alone or with other diabetes medicines. Depending on the study, Foundayo was used on its own or in combination with other diabetes medicines and was compared with placebo, dapagliflozin or oral semaglutide. The main measure of effectiveness was the change in HbA1c, a marker of blood glucose control. Across the studies, Foundayo reduced HbA1c by around 1.2 to 1.9 percentage points, depending on the dose received. This compared with reductions in HbA1c of 0.4 to 0.8 percentage points with placebo, 0.8 percentage points with dapagliflozin 10 mg and 1.2 to 1.5 percentage points with oral semaglutide, at doses of 7 mg and 14 mg, respectively. The most common side effects reported with Foundayo were nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, which occurred more often while the dose was increased and became less frequent over time. The opinion adopted by the CHMP is an intermediary step on Foundayo’s path to patient access. The opinion will now be sent to the European Commission for the adoption of a decision on an EU-wide marketing authorisation. Once a marketing authorisation has been granted, decisions about price and reimbursement will take place at the level of each Member State, taking into account the potential role or use of this medicine in the context of the national health system of that country. Notes The applicant for Foundayo is Eli Lilly Nederland B.V. Obese is defined as having a body mass index (BMI) of at least 30 kg / m2. Overweight is defined is having a BMI of least 27 kg / m2 but below 30 kg / m2. content: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 30, 2026 Contact: HHS Press Office 202-690-6343 Submit a Request for Comment HHS Announces LymeX Visible Voices Prize Winners WASHINGTON, D.C.—OCTOBER 30, 2026—The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) today announced 16 winners of the LymeX Visible Voices Prize, recognizing patient-informed resources that help patients, caregivers, and clinicians better understand Lyme and tickborne disease diagnosis.“Patients battling Lyme and other tickborne diseases deserve answers, and their experiences must drive our work,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “These winners turn patient insights into practical tools that help families and clinicians navigate diagnosis. Under President Trump’s leadership, we are mobilizing patients, researchers, and innovators through the Lyme Disease Moonshot to confront diagnostic challenges, advance treatment, and deliver the progress patients demand.”Drexel University College of Medicine received the $50,000 Grand Prize. Five Excellence Prizes of $20,000 each went to MyLymeCoach, The Visible Diagnosis Project, Global Lyme Alliance, Patient Powered Insights from MyLymeData, and Galaxy Diagnostics. Ten additional submissions received Impact Awards of $10,000 each.Visible Voices is one of four 2026 LymeX prize competitions supporting the HHS Lyme Disease Moonshot. It advances priorities outlined in President Trump’s Executive Order, Eliminating Disease-Carrying Pests and Restoring Enjoyment of the Great Outdoors, which directs HHS to build on the Lyme Moonshot through prize competitions or research and development.Winners were selected following nonfederal expert evaluation and federal review.Explore all winning submissions at LymeXVisibleVoicesPrize.com.Learn more about HHS Lyme disease initiatives at HHS.gov/Lyme. ### Note: All HHS press releases, fact sheets and other news materials are available in our Press Room.Like HHS on Facebook, follow HHS on X @HHSgov, @SecKennedy, and sign up for HHS Email Updates.Last revised: October 30, 2026

content: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 28, 2026 Contact: HHS Press Office 202-690-6343 Submit a Request for Comment A Real Food Halloween: Secretary Kennedy Joins Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas on The Real Food Show WASHINGTON, D.C.—OCTOBER 28, 2026—U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F.
